items.prompt: What is an SLI (Service Level Indicator), in this unit's terms?
choices: A concrete, measurable signal that reflects actual service health, like request success rate or a latency percentile
A raw resource metric like CPU utilization on its own
A contractual promise made to an external customer
The name of a monitoring dashboard tool
items.explanation: An SLI is a measurable signal tied to actual outcomes users experience — success rate, latency — not a raw resource number like CPU that may say nothing about whether users are being served correctly.
items.reference:
📈 SLI = measurable signal (e.g. success rate)
🎯 SLO = target threshold on that signal
📄 SLA = external contract, usually looser

Why: An SLI has to reflect real user impact, not just what's easy to instrument.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, twelve resource dashboards (CPU, memory, disk, network) were all green during a real 40-minute outage. Why didn't any of them qualify as a useful SLI for this incident?
choices: None of them were tied to whether users' requests actually succeeded — the failure showed up only in request success rate, a signal none of the twelve tracked
There weren't enough of them — the team needed twenty dashboards instead of twelve
Resource metrics are always useless and should never be monitored
The dashboards were displaying stale, outdated data
items.explanation: The twelve panels tracked infrastructure resources, not user-facing outcomes — a connection pool silently rejecting requests never moved CPU, memory, disk, or network into an abnormal range, so none of them could have served as the SLI that mattered.
items.reference:
📈 SLI = measurable signal (e.g. success rate)
🎯 SLO = target threshold on that signal
📄 SLA = external contract, usually looser

Why: An SLI has to reflect real user impact, not just what's easy to instrument.

items.prompt: Which of these is the best candidate SLI for a checkout service?
choices: The percentage of checkout requests that complete successfully
The number of lines of code in the checkout service
The total disk space available on the node hosting checkout
How many engineers are on the checkout team
items.explanation: A good SLI is a signal close to what a user directly experiences — whether their checkout request succeeded — rather than an internal resource or team-size number that may not correlate with user impact at all.
items.reference:
📈 SLI = measurable signal (e.g. success rate)
🎯 SLO = target threshold on that signal
📄 SLA = external contract, usually looser

Why: An SLI has to reflect real user impact, not just what's easy to instrument.

items.prompt: What is an SLO (Service Level Objective)?
choices: An internal target threshold on an SLI that a team commits to, e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days
The raw measured value of a metric at this exact moment
A synonym for an SLA with no meaningful difference
A dashboard panel showing CPU and memory usage
items.explanation: An SLO turns a raw SLI into a decision boundary — a target the team commits to internally, which is what makes it possible to say 'we are currently meeting our commitment' rather than just reporting a number with no context.
items.reference:
📈 SLI = measurable signal (e.g. success rate)
🎯 SLO = target threshold on that signal
📄 SLA = external contract, usually looser

Why: An SLO is what turns a raw number into a threshold worth acting on.

items.prompt: A team says "our request success rate is 99.94%." Is that statement, by itself, an SLO?
choices: No — that's an SLI reading. It only becomes meaningful as an SLO once compared against a committed target, like 99.9%
Yes — any measured percentage is automatically an SLO
No, because SLOs can only be set by an external customer, never internally
Yes, because SLOs are defined as whatever the current reading happens to be
items.explanation: 99.94% on its own is just a measurement (the SLI). It becomes an SLO comparison only once there's a committed target to check it against — otherwise there's no way to know whether 99.94% counts as "fine" or "a problem."
items.reference:
📈 SLI = measurable signal (e.g. success rate)
🎯 SLO = target threshold on that signal
📄 SLA = external contract, usually looser

Why: An SLO is what turns a raw number into a threshold worth acting on.

items.prompt: What is an SLA (Service Level Agreement)?
choices: An external, often contractual commitment to a customer, usually set looser than the internal SLO, with real consequences for breaching it
The same thing as an SLO, just a different name for internal use
A measurable signal like latency or success rate
A type of infrastructure dashboard
items.explanation: An SLA is a business-level, often contractual promise to an external party — distinct from the SLI (a raw signal) and the SLO (the internal target), and typically looser than the SLO to leave room to react before a breach.
items.reference:
📈 SLI = measurable signal (e.g. success rate)
🎯 SLO = target threshold on that signal
📄 SLA = external contract, usually looser

Why: The SLA is a business commitment layered on top of the SLO, not the same thing.

items.prompt: Why is an SLA typically set looser (a lower target) than the internal SLO for the same service?
choices: So the team has a buffer to notice and fix a problem via the tighter internal SLO before it becomes a contractual breach with real consequences
Because SLAs are always measured differently and can't be compared to SLOs at all
Because customers always demand looser numbers than engineers want internally
There's no reason — SLA and SLO should always be numerically identical
items.explanation: The gap between a tighter internal SLO and a looser external SLA is a deliberate buffer — crossing the SLO gives the team an early warning and time to react before also risking the SLA and its penalties.
items.reference:
📈 SLI = measurable signal (e.g. success rate)
🎯 SLO = target threshold on that signal
📄 SLA = external contract, usually looser

Why: The SLA is a business commitment layered on top of the SLO, not the same thing.

items.prompt: A company misses its SLA for the month. What is the typical real consequence, distinct from missing an internal SLO?
choices: A contractual consequence such as a service credit or penalty owed to the customer
Nothing — SLAs have no real consequences, unlike SLOs
The company's internal dashboards are automatically deleted
The SLO is automatically loosened to match the SLA going forward
items.explanation: An SLA breach carries an external, often financial consequence (credits, penalties) because it's a commitment made to a customer — that's the defining difference from an SLO miss, which is an internal signal to act, not a contractual event.
items.reference:
📈 SLI = measurable signal (e.g. success rate)
🎯 SLO = target threshold on that signal
📄 SLA = external contract, usually looser

Why: The SLA is a business commitment layered on top of the SLO, not the same thing.

items.prompt: Roughly how much downtime does a 99.9% availability SLO allow over a 30-day month?
choices: About 43 minutes
About 43 seconds
About 4.3 hours
Zero — 99.9% means no downtime is ever allowed
items.explanation: 0.1% of a 30-day month (43,200 minutes) is about 43.2 minutes — the error budget a 99.9% SLO implies for that window.
items.reference:
🧮 30 days = 43,200 minutes
➗ 0.1% of 43,200 ≈ 43 minutes

Why: The error budget is a real, spendable number derived directly from the SLO target.

items.prompt: What is the error budget, in this unit's framing?
choices: The amount of allowed failure an SLO implies, treated as a real, spendable resource for deciding how aggressively to ship risky changes
The monthly budget allocated to buy monitoring software licenses
A number that only matters for a compliance report, with no effect on day-to-day decisions
The total downtime a service has ever experienced across its entire history
items.explanation: The error budget isn't just a report-card number — it's meant to actively inform decisions like whether it's a good week to ship a risky change, the same way a real budget gets checked before an expense.
items.reference:
🧮 30 days = 43,200 minutes
➗ 0.1% of 43,200 ≈ 43 minutes

Why: The error budget is a real, spendable number derived directly from the SLO target.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, what actually caught the real problem, after the resource dashboards failed to?
choices: An engineer noticed it by accident while tailing raw logs, well after the failure had already been ongoing
An automated alert fired the moment the connection pool started rejecting requests
The SLA was breached, which automatically triggered an investigation
A scheduled weekly report flagged the anomaly
items.explanation: Nothing automated caught it — the team only found the real problem by chance, well into the incident, which is exactly the gap symptom-based alerting on the SLI is meant to close.
items.reference:
📊 12 dashboards checked: all green
🔥 real impact: ongoing for 40 minutes, unnoticed

Why: Green resource dashboards and a healthy service are two different claims.

items.prompt: Why did request success rate detect the Scenario's problem when CPU, memory, disk, and network did not?
choices: Because success rate directly reflects whether users' requests worked, while the failing connection pool never pushed any resource metric outside its normal range
Because success rate is measured more frequently than resource metrics
Because CPU, memory, disk, and network were being monitored on the wrong node entirely
Because resource metrics are never useful for detecting any kind of failure
items.explanation: The failure was specific to request handling (a connection pool rejecting requests), which resource utilization numbers simply didn't reflect — only a signal tied to actual request outcomes could catch it.
items.reference:
📊 12 dashboards checked: all green
🔥 real impact: ongoing for 40 minutes, unnoticed

Why: Green resource dashboards and a healthy service are two different claims.

items.prompt: What is the central lesson the Scenario is illustrating about infrastructure health?
choices: Every raw resource metric can look normal while real users are actively failing — infrastructure health has to be measured by user-facing outcomes, not just resource utilization
Resource dashboards should be deleted entirely since they're never useful
The team simply didn't have enough dashboards and needed more of them
The incident proves that request success rate is an unreliable signal
items.explanation: The point isn't "more dashboards" or "fewer dashboards" — it's that resource metrics and user-facing outcomes are different claims, and only the latter tells you whether infrastructure is actually doing its job.
items.reference:
📊 12 dashboards checked: all green
🔥 real impact: ongoing for 40 minutes, unnoticed

Why: Green resource dashboards and a healthy service are two different claims.

items.prompt: A team sets their internal SLO and their external SLA to the exact same number: 99.9% for both. What's the practical problem?
choices: There's no buffer between missing the internal target and being in contractual breach — the team only learns of a problem at the worst possible moment
There's no problem — matching numbers is the ideal setup
SLOs and SLAs can never legally be set to the same number
It would make the SLA impossible to measure at all
items.explanation: The gap between a tighter SLO and a looser SLA exists specifically to give the team early warning and time to react before the tighter external commitment (with its penalties) is also at risk.
items.reference:
🎯 SLO 99.9% (internal, tighter)
📄 SLA 99.5% (external, looser, penalties)

Why: The gap between them is a deliberate early-warning buffer.

items.prompt: Why does the SLA sit as a looser threshold than the SLO, rather than the other way around?
choices: The SLO is meant to trigger internal action before things get bad enough to also risk the external, penalty-bearing SLA
Because SLAs are always measured over a much shorter time window than SLOs
Because customers always negotiate for stricter numbers than engineers want
There's no real reason for the ordering — it's arbitrary convention
items.explanation: If the SLA were tighter than the SLO, the team would already be in contractual breach before their own internal target even flagged a problem — the ordering exists to give the internal signal a head start.
items.reference:
🎯 SLO 99.9% (internal, tighter)
📄 SLA 99.5% (external, looser, penalties)

Why: The gap between them is a deliberate early-warning buffer.

items.prompt: A service has a 99.9% SLO measured over a 30-day (43,200-minute) window. Roughly how many minutes of downtime does that allow?
choices: About 43.2 minutes
About 4.32 minutes
About 432 minutes
About 4,320 minutes
items.explanation: 0.1% (the allowed failure ratio) of 43,200 minutes is 43.2 minutes — the error budget for that window.
items.reference:
🧮 budget = window × (1 − SLO target)
📅 43,200 min × 0.001 = 43.2 min

Why: The same formula scales to any SLO target and any window length.

items.prompt: A service has a 99% SLO measured over a 7-day (10,080-minute) window. Roughly how many minutes of downtime does that allow?
choices: About 100.8 minutes
About 10.08 minutes
About 1,008 minutes
Zero, since 99% is already very high
items.explanation: 1% (the allowed failure ratio for a 99% SLO) of 10,080 minutes is about 100.8 minutes — a noticeably larger budget than a 99.9% SLO gets, since one fewer "9" is a 10x looser target.
items.reference:
🧮 budget = window × (1 − SLO target)
📅 43,200 min × 0.001 = 43.2 min

Why: The same formula scales to any SLO target and any window length.

items.prompt: Between a 99.9% SLO and a 99.99% SLO over the same 30-day window, which allows more downtime, and by roughly what factor?
choices: 99.9% allows roughly 10x more downtime than 99.99% (about 43 minutes vs. about 4.3 minutes)
They allow exactly the same amount of downtime
99.99% allows more downtime, since it looks like a bigger number
The relationship can't be determined without knowing the total number of requests
items.explanation: Each additional "9" in an SLO target divides the allowed failure ratio by 10, so 99.9% (0.1% allowed) permits about 10x the downtime of 99.99% (0.01% allowed) over the same window.
items.reference:
🧮 budget = window × (1 − SLO target)
📅 43,200 min × 0.001 = 43.2 min

Why: The same formula scales to any SLO target and any window length.

items.prompt: A team has already burned 38 of its 43-minute monthly error budget from one bad incident, with two weeks still left in the window. What's the most reasonable call about a moderately risky migration that's ready to ship?
choices: Delay it — with only about 5 minutes of budget left and two weeks to go, there's very little room left to absorb anything else going wrong
Ship it immediately regardless, since the budget is just a reporting artifact
The error budget has no bearing on this decision at all
Ship it immediately because burning the rest of the budget resets it early
items.explanation: With almost the entire budget already spent and weeks remaining in the window, taking on more risk right now is exactly the situation the error budget is meant to flag — this is a week to stabilize, not to ship something risky.
items.reference:
💰 budget left → room to ship riskier changes
🧯 budget spent → slow down, stabilize instead

Why: The budget is meant to be checked before deciding how much risk to take on, not just tallied afterward.

items.prompt: A team has 38 of its 43-minute monthly budget remaining, with only minor incidents so far. What's the reasonable call about a risky-but-valuable migration ready to ship?
choices: Ship it as planned — there's ample budget remaining to absorb the risk if something goes wrong
Refuse to ship anything risky for the rest of the month regardless of budget
The remaining budget is irrelevant to this decision
Wait for the SLA to be renegotiated before shipping anything
items.explanation: With most of the budget still unspent, there's real room to take on the migration's risk without meaningfully threatening the SLO for this window — this is exactly the situation where the budget supports moving forward.
items.reference:
💰 budget left → room to ship riskier changes
🧯 budget spent → slow down, stabilize instead

Why: The budget is meant to be checked before deciding how much risk to take on, not just tallied afterward.

items.prompt: Why does treating the error budget as just a compliance number to report upward miss the point of having one?
choices: Because its real value is informing a decision before the fact (how much risk to take on this week), not just summarizing after the fact how the month went
Because compliance reports are never accurate
Because error budgets are only meaningful once a quarter, not weekly
Because reporting the budget upward is illegal in most organizations
items.explanation: A budget checked only after the month ends can't influence any decision that already happened — the whole benefit comes from checking it beforehand, the same way a real budget gets checked before an expense, not just tallied afterward.
items.reference:
💰 budget left → room to ship riskier changes
🧯 budget spent → slow down, stabilize instead

Why: The budget is meant to be checked before deciding how much risk to take on, not just tallied afterward.

items.prompt: What does "symptom-based alerting" mean in this unit?
choices: Alerting on the SLI itself — the user-facing signal — rather than on every raw resource metric individually
Alerting only when a customer files a support ticket
Alerting on every possible resource metric simultaneously, to be maximally thorough
Disabling all alerts and relying entirely on manual dashboard checks
items.explanation: Symptom-based alerting targets the signal that directly reflects user impact — request success rate burning through the error budget — instead of a flood of individual raw-metric thresholds that may not correlate with real impact at all.
items.reference:
🚨 alert on the SLI (user-facing signal)
🔇 not on every individual raw resource metric

Why: The SLI is the one signal that's already been chosen to reflect real user impact.

items.prompt: What two failure modes does alerting on every individual raw resource metric produce at once?
choices: It can miss real problems that don't cross any single resource threshold, while also producing noisy alerts for fluctuations that never actually affected users
It's slower to configure than symptom-based alerting, but otherwise equally effective
It only ever produces false negatives, never false positives
It's identical in effect to symptom-based alerting, just phrased differently
items.explanation: Raw-metric alerting misses failures like a connection pool rejecting requests without moving any resource metric abnormally, while simultaneously firing on harmless resource blips that never reach users — both are real costs of the same wrong layer.
items.reference:
🚨 alert on the SLI (user-facing signal)
🔇 not on every individual raw resource metric

Why: The SLI is the one signal that's already been chosen to reflect real user impact.

items.prompt: In the Scenario's incident, why would a single alert on request success rate have been more useful than twelve separate resource-metric alerts?
choices: Because success rate dropping from 99.95% to 83% is one unambiguous signal that something is actually wrong for users, while none of the twelve resource metrics ever crossed a threshold at all
Because a single alert is always technically easier to configure in monitoring software
Because resource-metric alerts are always disabled by default
Because success rate alerts never produce false positives under any circumstances
items.explanation: The success-rate drop was the one signal directly reflecting real impact — a single alert on it would have fired immediately, while the twelve resource dashboards stayed green the entire time because none of them measured the thing that actually broke.
items.reference:
🚨 alert on the SLI (user-facing signal)
🔇 not on every individual raw resource metric

Why: The SLI is the one signal that's already been chosen to reflect real user impact.

items.prompt: How does alert fatigue from noisy raw-metric alerting connect to `test-suite-architecture`'s theme about flaky tests?
choices: Both describe the same trust-erosion pattern: a signal that fires too often for things that don't matter eventually gets ignored, muted, or distrusted entirely
They are unrelated concepts that happen to share the word "alert"
Flaky tests and noisy alerts are the same technical mechanism under the hood
`test-suite-architecture` argues that alerting is unnecessary if tests are trustworthy
items.explanation: A flaky test that fails for reasons unrelated to real bugs gets ignored the same way a noisy alert firing on harmless resource blips gets muted — in both cases, over-triggering on non-issues erodes trust in the signal itself.
items.reference:
🧪 flaky test fires often for non-issues → ignored
🚨 noisy alert fires often for non-issues → muted

Why: Any signal that cries wolf too often stops being trusted, regardless of the domain.

items.prompt: Why does alerting on the SLI directly (rather than every raw metric) help keep every alert that does fire worth waking up for?
choices: Because the SLI has already been chosen specifically to reflect real user impact, so an alert on it is inherently more likely to correspond to something that actually matters
Because SLI-based alerts are technically incapable of ever being false positives
Because raw-metric alerts are always more accurate than SLI-based alerts
Because SLIs change less frequently than raw metrics, so there are fewer alerts overall regardless of accuracy
items.explanation: The SLI was deliberately picked because it tracks real user outcomes — alerting on it means each alert is grounded in actual impact, which is what keeps on-call trusting that a page means something, unlike a flood of raw-metric noise.
items.reference:
🧪 flaky test fires often for non-issues → ignored
🚨 noisy alert fires often for non-issues → muted

Why: Any signal that cries wolf too often stops being trusted, regardless of the domain.

items.prompt: Complete `computeErrorBudget(sloTarget, windowMinutes)` so it returns the allowed downtime in minutes, rounded to 2 decimal places: `windowMinutes * (1 - sloTarget)`, rounded. Throw an Error if `sloTarget` is not strictly between 0 and 1.

tests.description: 99.9% SLO over 43,200 minutes (30 days) allows 43.2 minutes
99.9% SLO over 10,080 minutes (7 days) allows 10.08 minutes

items.explanation: The budget is a direct application of the SLO's allowed failure ratio to the window length; rounding to 2 decimals avoids floating-point noise from subtracting values like 0.999 from 1 while keeping the result precise enough to be meaningful.
items.reference:
🧮 budget = window × (1 − SLO target)
⚠️ invalid target (0 or 1) → throw

Why: A target of exactly 0 or 1 isn't a meaningful SLO — it permits either total failure or literal zero tolerance.

items.prompt: Complete `computeErrorBudget(sloTarget, windowMinutes)` so it returns the allowed downtime in minutes, rounded to 2 decimal places: `windowMinutes * (1 - sloTarget)`, rounded. Throw an Error if `windowMinutes` is not a positive number.
items.explanation: A window of zero or negative minutes has no meaningful budget to compute, so validating it up front prevents a nonsensical or misleading result from ever being returned to a caller.
items.reference:
🧮 budget = window × (1 − SLO target)
⚠️ invalid target (0 or 1) → throw

Why: A target of exactly 0 or 1 isn't a meaningful SLO — it permits either total failure or literal zero tolerance.

items.prompt: Complete `computeConsumedMinutes(failedRequests, totalRequests, elapsedMinutes)` so it returns `elapsedMinutes * (failedRequests / totalRequests)`, rounded to 2 decimal places. Throw an Error if `totalRequests` is not greater than 0.

tests.description: 35,000 of 500,000 failed over 7,200 elapsed minutes consumes 504 minutes
500 of 10,000 failed over 1,440 elapsed minutes consumes 72 minutes

items.explanation: Scaling elapsed time by the observed failure ratio converts a request-based SLI into the same time-denominated units the error budget is expressed in, without needing to track literal outage intervals.
items.reference:
🧮 consumed = elapsed minutes × failure ratio
📉 7% failing over 7,200 min ⇒ 504 min consumed

Why: This turns a success-rate SLI into the same time units the SLO's budget is expressed in.

items.prompt: Complete `computeRemainingMinutes(totalBudgetMinutes, failedRequests, totalRequests, elapsedMinutes)` so it returns the remaining budget: `totalBudgetMinutes - (elapsedMinutes * failedRequests / totalRequests)`, rounded to 2 decimal places. The result can be negative if the budget is already over-spent.

tests.description: a budget that is fully over-spent returns a negative number

items.explanation: The remaining budget is simply the total minus whatever's already been consumed — allowing it to go negative is deliberate, since a negative remainder is exactly what signals the budget has been fully spent and then some.
items.reference:
🧮 consumed = elapsed minutes × failure ratio
📉 7% failing over 7,200 min ⇒ 504 min consumed

Why: This turns a success-rate SLI into the same time units the SLO's budget is expressed in.

items.prompt: Complete `computeBurnRate(observedFailureRatio, allowedFailureRatio)` so it returns `observedFailureRatio / allowedFailureRatio`, rounded to 2 decimal places. Throw an Error if `allowedFailureRatio` is not greater than 0.

tests.description: 12% failing against a 0.1% allowance burns at 120x
0.3% failing against a 0.1% allowance burns at 3x

items.explanation: Burn rate is a ratio of the currently-observed failure rate to the rate an SLO can sustainably tolerate — a value of 1 means spending the budget exactly on pace to exhaust it by the end of the window, and higher values mean faster.
items.reference:
🐢 burn rate 1 = sustainable pace
🔥 burn rate 120 = budget gone in hours, not weeks

Why: A high burn rate deserves urgency even if little absolute budget is spent yet.

items.prompt: Complete `hoursUntilBudgetExhausted(burnRate, windowHours)` so it returns how many hours it would take to fully exhaust the budget at the given burn rate: `windowHours / burnRate`, rounded to 2 decimal places. Throw an Error if `burnRate` is not greater than 0.

tests.description: a 30-day (720-hour) window burning at 120x empties in 6 hours
the same window burning at 1x (sustainable) takes the full 720 hours

items.explanation: A burn rate of N means the budget is being spent N times faster than the rate that would exactly last the whole window, so dividing the window by the burn rate gives the actual time until exhaustion at that rate.
items.reference:
🐢 burn rate 1 = sustainable pace
🔥 burn rate 120 = budget gone in hours, not weeks

Why: A high burn rate deserves urgency even if little absolute budget is spent yet.

items.prompt: A service is burning its error budget at a fast, severe rate right now, but has consumed only a small absolute percentage of the budget so far. Should it be paged immediately?
choices: Yes — a fast burn rate means the entire budget will be exhausted soon if the rate continues, regardless of how little has been spent so far
No — small absolute consumption always means it's safe to wait
No — burn rate is irrelevant, only the absolute percentage consumed matters
It depends only on which day of the month it is, not on the burn rate
items.explanation: Burn rate measures how fast the budget is being spent right now — a severe rate can exhaust the entire budget in hours even if very little has technically been consumed yet, which is exactly why it deserves urgency despite a small absolute number.
items.reference:
🐢 slow burn: similar % consumed over days — investigate later
🔥 fast burn: budget gone in hours — page now

Why: Rate, not just amount, is what tells you how urgent the response needs to be.

items.prompt: Two services have both consumed 5% of their monthly error budget. One did it in the last 20 minutes; the other did it gradually over the last two weeks. Do they deserve the same alerting response?
choices: No — the one that burned 5% in 20 minutes has a far higher burn rate and is heading toward exhausting its entire budget much sooner if it continues
Yes — since the percentage consumed is identical, the urgency is identical
No, but only because one of them must have a lower SLO target than the other
Yes — burn rate has no bearing on how urgently a team should respond
items.explanation: Identical percentage consumed can come from very different rates — 5% in 20 minutes projects to exhausting the full budget in a fraction of the window, while 5% over two weeks is on a much more sustainable trajectory, even though the absolute amounts consumed so far are the same.
items.reference:
🐢 slow burn: similar % consumed over days — investigate later
🔥 fast burn: budget gone in hours — page now

Why: Rate, not just amount, is what tells you how urgent the response needs to be.

items.prompt: Why is a burn rate of exactly 1 described as "sustainable, if unwelcome" rather than "fine"?
choices: Because it means the budget is on pace to be fully exhausted right at the end of the window — technically within bounds, but with zero margin left for anything else going wrong
Because a burn rate of 1 always indicates a severe, ongoing incident
Because a burn rate of 1 means the SLO has already been breached
Because burn rate values below 1 are impossible to observe in practice
items.explanation: A burn rate of 1 uses up the entire budget exactly on schedule — it doesn't breach the SLO, but it also leaves no room for any additional failure for the rest of the window, which is why it's sustainable but still worth watching.
items.reference:
🐢 slow burn: similar % consumed over days — investigate later
🔥 fast burn: budget gone in hours — page now

Why: Rate, not just amount, is what tells you how urgent the response needs to be.

items.prompt: What real problem does an SLO set too loose (e.g. 99% on a checkout flow where any failure matters a lot) cause?
choices: False confidence — the org believes it's meeting its reliability bar while real users experience meaningful, uncounted pain that never burns enough budget to trigger action
It has no downside as long as the number is technically met
It makes the SLA impossible to define at all
It always causes the team to ship too slowly
items.explanation: A loose SLO can be "met" while still permitting a meaningful amount of real user pain — 99% on a 30-day month allows over 7 hours of failure, which can matter enormously for a purchase flow while looking fine on paper.
items.reference:
😌 too loose → false confidence, real pain goes uncounted
😰 too strict → unmeetable, or forces overly conservative shipping

Why: The right SLO is set from what matters to users and what infrastructure can realistically sustain.

items.prompt: What real problem does an SLO set too strict (unrealistic given the service's actual failure modes) cause?
choices: It either can't realistically be met, or it forces the team into overly conservative, slow shipping just to avoid ever touching the budget
It has no downside — stricter is always strictly better
It automatically converts into a looser SLA over time
It makes the error budget calculation mathematically impossible
items.explanation: An SLO set beyond what the infrastructure can realistically sustain either gets quietly ignored once the team stops trusting it, or drives excessive caution that slows shipping down far more than the actual reliability need justifies.
items.reference:
😌 too loose → false confidence, real pain goes uncounted
😰 too strict → unmeetable, or forces overly conservative shipping

Why: The right SLO is set from what matters to users and what infrastructure can realistically sustain.

items.prompt: What should actually determine where an SLO's target is set, according to this unit?
choices: What genuinely matters to users, balanced against what the infrastructure can realistically sustain — not whichever number sounds most impressive
Whichever number is easiest to calculate the error budget for
The highest possible number, since more nines are always strictly better regardless of cost
A number chosen independently of both user impact and infrastructure reality, purely by convention
items.explanation: Both directions of getting the SLO wrong (too loose or too strict) stem from disconnecting the target from those two real anchors — user impact and realistic sustainability — rather than from picking an arbitrary or impressive-sounding number.
items.reference:
😌 too loose → false confidence, real pain goes uncounted
😰 too strict → unmeetable, or forces overly conservative shipping

Why: The right SLO is set from what matters to users and what infrastructure can realistically sustain.

items.prompt: Why does the burn-rate alerting function require the burn rate to be elevated in both a short window and a longer window before paging, rather than the short window alone?
choices: To filter out brief blips that spike the short window but self-resolve before meaningfully affecting the longer window, avoiding the alert-fatigue pattern of paging for non-issues
Because short windows are technically incapable of measuring burn rate accurately
Because long windows always produce higher burn-rate values than short windows
There's no real reason — it's an arbitrary implementation detail
items.explanation: A brief blip can spike the short window's burn rate without ever meaningfully affecting the longer window, since it resolves quickly — requiring both windows to agree filters that noise out while still catching a real, sustained incident quickly.
items.reference:
⏱️ short window alone: catches real incidents fast, but also noise
📆 long window too: filters brief blips that self-resolve

Why: A page that fires for non-issues erodes trust the same way a flaky test does.

items.prompt: What would happen if the alerting function paged based on the short window's burn rate alone, ignoring the long window entirely?
choices: It would page for brief, self-resolving blips as often as for genuine sustained incidents, which erodes on-call's trust in the alert over time
It would become strictly more accurate than the two-window version
It would stop being able to detect any real incidents at all
It would have no practical difference from the two-window version
items.explanation: A short-window-only trigger fires on transient spikes as readily as on real, sustained problems — over time, on-call learns that a page doesn't reliably mean something serious, which is the exact trust erosion the alert-fatigue theme from testing-quality describes.
